text: In a photoelectric experiment, doubling the intensity of incident light (keeping frequency constant, above threshold) has what effect?
options: The maximum kinetic energy of each photoelectron doubles, but the number of photoelectrons remains unchanged.
Both the number of photoelectrons and their maximum kinetic energy double.
The number of photoelectrons emitted per second doubles, but the maximum kinetic energy of each photoelectron remains unchanged.
Neither the number of photoelectrons nor their kinetic energy changes, since intensity doesn't affect the photoelectric effect.
correct_answer: The number of photoelectrons emitted per second doubles, but the maximum kinetic energy of each photoelectron remains unchanged.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: In the photoelectric effect, intensity determines the number of photons arriving per second, while frequency alone determines each photon's energy.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the separate roles of intensity and frequency

solution_steps.step_text: Select: number of photoelectrons ∝ intensity; maximum KE depends only on frequency (via KE_max = hν − W).
Substitute: doubling intensity doubles the photon arrival rate, while ν (and hence KE_max) is unchanged.
Conclude: the number of photoelectrons per second doubles; the maximum kinetic energy stays the same.

The maximum kinetic energy of each photo.misconception: swapped which quantity depends on intensity vs frequency, a classic misconception

Both the number of photoelectrons and th.misconception: assumed both quantities scale with intensity, ignoring that KE depends only on frequency

Neither the number of photoelectrons nor.misconception: a conceptual overcorrection, incorrectly believing intensity has no effect at all

text: In a photoelectric experiment, light of frequency 1×10¹⁵ Hz produces a stopping potential of 2.07 V. Using h=4.14×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s, find the work function, then find the new stopping potential when the frequency is increased to 1.5×10¹⁵ Hz.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The work function can first be found from the given frequency and stopping potential, then reused to find the new stopping potential at the new frequency.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the two-step work function then new stopping potential calculation

solution_steps.step_text: Select W = hν1 − eV01, then eV02 = hν2 − W.
solution_steps.formula_used: W = hν1 − eV01; eV02 = hν2 − W
W = hν1 − eV01; eV02 = hν2 − W

solution_steps.step_text: Compute V02 = 4.14 V.

6.21 V.misconception: forgot to subtract the work function for the new frequency, reporting the new photon energy directly

2.07 V.misconception: assumed the stopping potential stays unchanged regardless of the frequency increase

8.28 V.misconception: added the work function to the new photon energy instead of subtracting

text: In a photoelectric experiment, a graph of stopping potential V0 versus frequency ν gives a straight line with slope 4.14×10⁻¹⁵ V·s, intersecting the frequency axis (V0=0) at ν=5×10¹⁴ Hz. Find Planck's constant h (in eV·s) and the work function W (in eV).
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Einstein's photoelectric equation, rewritten as V0 = (h/e)ν − (W/e), is a straight line whose slope gives h/e and whose frequency-intercept relates to W.
Select: slope = h (in eV·s, since V0 is in volts), and at the x-intercept, 0 = hν0 − W, so W = hν0.
Substitute slope = 4.14×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s directly as h. With ν0 = 5×10¹⁴ Hz: W = 4.14×10⁻¹⁵×5×10¹⁴.
Compute h = 4.14×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s, and W = 2.07 eV.

h = 4.14×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s, W = 4.14 eV.misconception: correctly found h but incorrectly reported it again as W, forgetting to multiply by the frequency intercept

h = 5×10¹⁴ eV·s, W = 2.07 eV.misconception: swapped the roles of the slope and the x-intercept, mistakenly treating the frequency intercept value as if it were h

h = 4.14×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s, W = 20.7 eV.misconception: correctly found h but misplaced a decimal in the frequency intercept, using 5×10¹⁵ instead of the given 5×10¹⁴

text: Find the momentum of a photon with wavelength 500 nm. Use h=6.6×10⁻³⁴ J·s.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: A photon carries momentum related to its wavelength, following the same relation as de Broglie's formula.
Select p = h/λ.
Compute p = 1.32×10⁻²⁷ kg·m/s.

text: An electron and a photon have the same de Broglie wavelength of 2×10⁻¹⁰ m. Find the momentum of the electron. Use h=6.6×10⁻³⁴ J·s.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The de Broglie relation p=h/λ applies to any particle, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta regardless of particle type.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying that de Broglie momentum depends only on wavelength

solution_steps.step_text: Select p = h/λ.
Substitute h = 6.6×10⁻³⁴ J·s, λ = 2×10⁻¹⁰ m: p = 6.6×10⁻³⁴/(2×10⁻¹⁰).
Compute p = 3.3×10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.

6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.misconception: arithmetic slip, doubling the correct answer

text: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V, achieving a de Broglie wavelength λ. Find the new potential difference (in terms of V) required to halve the wavelength to λ/2.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: For an electron accelerated through a potential V, the de Broglie wavelength depends on V through an inverse square-root relationship.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the wavelength-voltage relation for accelerated electrons

solution_steps.step_text: Select λ ∝ 1/√V, so V ∝ 1/λ², giving V_new/V = (λ/λ_new)².
Substitute λ_new = λ/2: V_new/V = (λ/(λ/2))² = 2².
Compute V_new = 4V.

2V.misconception: forgot to square the ratio, using V∝1/λ directly instead of the correct V∝1/λ²

V/4.misconception: inverted the proportionality, assuming V∝λ² instead of V∝1/λ²

V/2.misconception: both inverted the proportionality and forgot to square it, assuming V∝λ directly

text: Find the speed of an electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen, given that the speed formula is v_n=(2.18×10⁶/n) m/s.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The orbital speed of an electron in the nth Bohr orbit decreases inversely with n.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the Bohr orbital speed formula

solution_steps.step_text: Select v_n = (2.18×10⁶/n) m/s.
Substitute n = 1: v_1 = 2.18×10⁶/1.
Compute v_1 = 2.18×10⁶ m/s.

text: An electron in a hydrogen atom is in the n=3 orbit. Using E_n=−13.6/n² eV, find the ionization energy required to remove this electron from the atom.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Ionization energy is the energy needed to bring the electron from its current level to n=∞ (where energy is zero), which equals the magnitude of the electron's current binding energy.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying ionization energy as the magnitude of the current energy level

solution_steps.step_text: Select ionization energy = |E_n| = 13.6/n².
Substitute n = 3: ionization energy = 13.6/9.
Compute ionization energy ≈ 1.51 eV.

text: The K absorption edge wavelength of an element is 0.4 Å. Using hc=12400 eV·Å, find this binding energy in keV.

text: A nucleus X (mass number 240) has a binding energy per nucleon of 7.6 MeV. It undergoes fission into two fragments of mass number 120 each, with a binding energy per nucleon of 8.5 MeV for each fragment. Find the total energy released.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The energy released equals the increase in total binding energy from the initial nucleus to the two final fragments.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the energy release from binding energy change

solution_steps.step_text: Select energy released = (total final BE) − (total initial BE).
Substitute: initial BE = 240×7.6 = 1824 MeV. Final BE = 2×(120×8.5) = 2×1020 = 2040 MeV.
Compute energy released = 2040 − 1824 = 216 MeV.

text: A radioactive nucleus undergoes alpha decay. Find the change in mass number and atomic number of the resulting daughter nucleus compared to the parent.
options: Mass number decreases by 2; atomic number decreases by 4.
Mass number decreases by 4; atomic number increases by 2.

correct_answer: Mass number decreases by 4; atomic number decreases by 2.

text: A radioactive sample decays such that 87.5% of the original sample has decayed after 30 minutes. Find the half-life of the sample.

text: In a nuclear reactor, each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases approximately 200 MeV of energy. Find the number of fissions per second required to produce a power output of 3.2×10¹⁰ W. (1 MeV=1.6×10⁻¹³ J)

text: A p-n junction diode with reverse saturation current 2 μA is operated in reverse bias, below its breakdown voltage. Find the current flowing through the circuit.
options: Depends on the exact reverse voltage applied, increasing proportionally with voltage
Very large, since reverse bias allows unrestricted current flow
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: In reverse bias, below the breakdown voltage, a diode conducts only a small, nearly constant reverse saturation current, largely independent of the applied voltage.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the reverse saturation current behavior

solution_steps.step_text: Select: reverse current ≈ reverse saturation current, for any reverse voltage below breakdown.
Substitute the given reverse saturation current of 2 μA into this relationship.
Conclude the current is 2 μA.

0 A.misconception: assumed reverse bias completely blocks all current, forgetting that a small reverse saturation current always flows

text: A silicon diode (barrier potential 0.7 V) and a germanium diode (barrier potential 0.3 V) are connected in parallel with the same polarity, then in series with a 100 Ω resistor to a 10 V battery in the forward direction. Assuming both diodes are ideal beyond their barrier potentials, find the voltage across the parallel diode combination and the current through the resistor.
options: Voltage across combination = 0.7 V; Current = 93 mA
Voltage across combination = 0.5 V; Current = 95 mA
Voltage across combination = 1.0 V; Current = 90 mA
Voltage across combination = 0.3 V; Current = 97 mA
correct_answer: Voltage across combination = 0.3 V; Current = 97 mA
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Two diodes in parallel must share the same voltage; the diode with the lower barrier potential (germanium) starts conducting first and clamps the voltage there, keeping the silicon diode off.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying which diode dominates in a parallel configuration

solution_steps.step_text: Select: voltage across the combination = lower barrier potential (germanium's 0.3 V), then V_resistor = V_battery − V_combination, and I = V_resistor/R.
Substitute V_battery = 10 V, V_combination = 0.3 V, R = 100 Ω: V_resistor = 10−0.3 = 9.7 V. I = 9.7/100.
Compute I = 97 mA, with the combination voltage at 0.3 V.

Voltage across combination = 0.7 V; Curr.misconception: assumed the silicon diode, with the higher barrier potential, dominates and conducts instead — but in parallel, the diode with the lower barrier potential conducts first and clamps the voltage

Voltage across combination = 0.5 V; Curr.misconception: incorrectly averaged the two barrier potentials instead of recognizing that the lower one dominates in a parallel configuration

Voltage across combination = 1.0 V; Curr.misconception: incorrectly added the two barrier potentials together, as if the diodes were connected in series rather than parallel
